title: [Full Workshop] Building Metrics that actually work — David Karam, Pi Labs (fmr Google Search)

summary: The workshop opens with audience discussion about evaluation challenges: defining correct answers, manual review burden, use-case uniqueness, validation consuming up to 80% of development time, and unreliable LLM-as-judge. David Karam and his co-presenter, both with over a decade at Google Search, frame evals as an ongoing methodology where domain knowledge lives. Google Search used approximately 300 metrics. They advocate progressively layering techniques by complexity and ROI: vibe testing, tracing, code-based checks, LLM-as-judge, and ultimately a scoring system starting with 5-10 correlated signals. Standard evals (helpfulness, harmfulness, hallucinations) serve as guardrails but fail at nuanced quality. A scoring system breaks subjective quality into many objective, inspectable signals combined into a single weighted score. The co-pilot demo shows generating synthetic good and bad examples, adding/removing dimensions, and editing Python code. Metrics are framed as either calibrated or uncalibrated rather than good or bad. Google Sheets integration lets participants run scorers on ~120 examples and view a confusion matrix showing alignment with real thumbs-up/thumbs-down labels. For production, scorers are designed for online workflows, scoring 20 dimensions in sub-50 milliseconds. The scoring models differ from decoder LLMs: they use bidirectional attention, a regression head instead of autoregressive token generation, and are trained on billions of tokens for scoring, yielding high precision and low variance. Calibration uses a generalized additive model that learns weights from thumbs-up/down data, including critical-fail logic. The workshop concludes with hands-on Colab exercises where participants copy their scoring spec into a pre-prepared notebook. The Colab loads public Hugging Face datasets with thumbs-up/thumbs-down data, runs the scorer, and builds confusion matrices. Three key exercises demonstrate practical applications: (1) model comparison across 5 models using ~10 examples, showing 2.5 slightly outperforms 1.5 but with minimal delta for reasoning tasks while smaller models like Claude Haiku show bigger quality deltas; (2) prompt regression testing by comparing bad and good system prompts against the scoring spec; (3) online best-of-N sampling where increasing from one response (temperature .7) to 3-4 responses, ranking them with the Pi scoring system, and picking the best shows steadily improving scores.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.
temporalContext: Transcript claims reflect the publication date; linked external context was checked at the run's research date.
takeaways: Evals are the primary place where domain knowledge lives; everything else (prompts, fine-tuning, online selection) builds on top of them.
Metrics are either calibrated or uncalibrated, not inherently good or bad; correlation analysis against ground truth is the core methodology.
A scoring system decomposes subjective quality into many objective, inspectable signals (NL questions or Python code) combined into a single weighted score, reducing variance and enabling slicing.
The scoring models use bidirectional attention and a regression head rather than autoregressive token generation, yielding high precision and sub-50ms scoring for ~20 dimensions.
Calibration via a generalized additive model learns which signals matter from thumbs-up/down data, including critical-fail logic where failing one signal fails everything.
Start with 5-10 simple correlated signals and iteratively add more; Google Search used ~300 metrics.
With reliable metrics, the rest of the stack simplifies: DSPy-style prompt optimization, synthetic data filtering, and online best-of-N selection become viable.
Google Sheets and Colab integration lets you run scorers on labeled data and inspect confusion matrices to measure alignment with real user feedback.
Scorers are designed for online production workflows, unlike expensive LLM-as-judge which cannot run online at scale.

The Colab workflow demonstrates three practical applications of a single scoring spec: multi-model comparison, prompt regression testing, and online best-of-N sampling with increasing response counts.

sections.title: Audience Q&A on Evals Challenges
sections.summary: The presenters poll the audience about evals experience and pain points. Attendees raise challenges including difficulty defining correct answers, labor-intensive manual review, the uniqueness of each AI use case preventing reuse, validation consuming up to 80% of development time, and questions about synthetic data for novel problems.

sections.title: Presenters' Background and Google Methodology
sections.summary: David and co-presenter introduce their decade-plus experience at Google Search, where evals were part of a broader 'quality' discipline. Google Search used approximately 300 metrics. They emphasize methodology: setting up benchmarks, calibrating metrics with humans and user data, and treating evals as an ongoing development practice. Resources at pi.ai/workshop and a Slack channel are announced.

sections.title: Progressive Evaluation Techniques and Scoring Systems
sections.summary: The presenters outline a progression of evaluation approaches: vibe testing, human evals, code-based checks, LLM-as-judge, and ultimately a scoring system. They stress starting with 5-10 simple correlated signals and building iteratively. LLM-as-judge is noted as difficult due to decoder models' creative design. No single approach is right or wrong — techniques are layered by complexity and ROI.

sections.title: Evals as Domain Knowledge and Online Techniques
sections.summary: The presenters argue evals are the primary place where domain knowledge lives, not just testing. With good evals you can use optimizers like DSPy to improve prompts, filter synthetic data for fine-tuning, and apply online techniques such as generating 4-5 responses at high temperature and scoring them to pick the best—a technique all big labs use. Standard evals (helpfulness, harmfulness, hallucinations) only serve as guardrails; nuanced quality requires custom metrics.

sections.title: Scoring System Concept and Benefits
sections.summary: A scoring system breaks subjective quality into many objective, inspectable signals—like Google Search decomposing ranking into SEO, popularity, title scores, content quality, spam, etc.—combined into a single score. Bottom-level signals are deterministic and objective (sometimes Python code); top-level combination is subjective. Benefits include reduced variance, higher precision, fine-grained slicing, and iterative signal addition.

sections.title: Co-pilot Demo and Workshop Structure
sections.summary: The presenters demo a co-pilot for building a scoring system, starting from a system prompt for a meeting summarizer that produces structured JSON with action items, insights, and a title. Users can start from system prompts, examples, or criteria. The tool generates individual dimensions as natural language questions or editable Python code sent to specialized scoring foundation models, with critical/major/minor weights.

sections.title: Calibration Philosophy and Co-pilot Example Generation
sections.summary: The presenters emphasize that metrics are either calibrated or uncalibrated, not inherently good or bad. Once you have metrics you can trust, the rest of the stack simplifies radically. The co-pilot can generate synthetic examples (good and bad, including broken JSON) from the system prompt, score them, and let users inspect individual dimension scores. Users can also ask the co-pilot to modify Python code, add or remove dimensions, and iterate human-in-the-loop. Most production clients run batch processes in Colab at scale.

sections.title: Google Sheets Integration and Confusion Matrix
sections.summary: The presenters demonstrate the Google Sheets integration: users copy criteria from the co-pilot into a pre-filled spreadsheet, select input/output rows, and run the scorer via an extensions menu. The scorer runs across approximately 120 examples and produces a confusion matrix showing alignment counts for thumbs-up, thumbs-down, and no-alignment cases. Users can modify dimensions or data directly in the sheet and re-score to improve alignment.

sections.title: Production Scale and Online Workflows
sections.summary: Addressing audience questions about scale, the presenters explain that scorers are designed for online workflows, evaluating ~20 dimensions in sub-50 milliseconds. Google ran most quality checks (spam detection, ranking decisions) online. LLM-as-judge is too expensive to run online, which this approach solves. Best practice is to sample from production logs, create eval sets with hard/medium/easy examples, and run scoring online or in batch.

sections.title: Scoring Model Architecture, Calibration, and Language Support
sections.summary: The scoring models differ from decoder LLMs: they use bidirectional attention, a regression head instead of autoregressive token generation, and are trained on billions of scoring-specific tokens. This yields high precision, low variance, and dense embeddings with fewer parameters. There is no prompt tuning—users ask a question and get an inspectable score. Signals are combined via a generalized additive model calibrated on thumbs-up/down data, learning which signals are critical-fail (e.g., spam) versus non-contributory. Current language support is English and a few languages; multilingual is on the roadmap. No multimodal support yet.

sections.title: Colab Workshop Exercises: Model Comparison, Prompt Testing, and Online Sampling
sections.summary: The workshop transitions to hands-on Colab exercises. Participants copy their scoring spec (natural language with Python code) from the co-pilot into a pre-prepared Colab notebook. The Colab loads public Hugging Face datasets with thumbs-up/thumbs-down data, runs the scorer, and builds confusion matrices. Three key exercises demonstrate practical applications: (1) Model comparison across 5 models using ~10 examples, showing 2.5 slightly outperforms 1.5 but with minimal delta for reasoning tasks, while smaller models like Claude Haiku show bigger quality deltas. (2) Prompt regression testing by comparing bad and good system prompts against the scoring spec to ensure no regression when changing prompts. (3) Online best-of-N sampling where increasing from one response (temperature .7) to 3-4 responses, ranking them with the Pi scoring system, and picking the best shows steadily improving scores as sample count increases.
